articles.title: I travel 200,000 miles a year. These are the five carry-on suitcases I actually trust
articles.summary: In an endless sea of suitcase options, these are the best to save you time and money. The best travel backpack. Sign up for the Filter US newsletter, your weekly guide to buying fewer, better things.
body: There are few worse feelings than climbing off an all-day flight, shambling on down to baggage claim, and then watching each and every one of your fellow passengers gleefully grab their bag and disappear, while yours is nowhere to be found. The devastating realization that your checked suitcase didn’t make it is a strong enough blow to turn the sweetest of vacations sour.

I’ve been there, and that’s just one of the many reasons I never check a bag unless I absolutely have to. But living the carry-on life requires having the right suitcase, and there are hundreds and hundreds of choices out there. We tested 15 models and considered dozens more to find the perfect one for you.

I make my living as a freelance journalist, but finding the story often means hopping on a plane and jetting somewhere far away. I fly about 200,000 miles every year, endure 150 days away from home, and set down in a dozen countries or more.

articles.title: Judith Lucy on her cancer diagnosis: ‘I’m a bit over getting so much material out of my life’
articles.summary: One of Australia’s hardest-working comedians is still laughing at the timing of a breast cancer diagnosis just as she set out to launch a book about wellness. Two days out from surgery, she talks burnout, Buddhism and saying goodbye to her boobs. Get our weekend culture and lifestyle email.
body: Judith Lucy cannot get a cold. A few hours before I’m due to meet her for a walk around the rose gardens and classic conservatory of the St Kilda Botanical Gardens, a stone’s throw from her home in Melbourne’s south-east, the beloved comedian is on a telehealth call from the front seat of her publicist’s car.

Her doctor needs to go over the results from the previous day’s scans to confirm everything is looking good – good enough to perform the double mastectomy they have planned for Friday, three weeks after she was diagnosed with breast cancer. The cancer isn’t appearing anywhere else on the scans, she learns, but a compromised immune system going into surgery would throw the whole thing out of whack. So with the blustery wind and grey skies at our backs, we retreat into her home instead. The walk up and down the hallway, from the front door of her lovely weatherboard cottage to the neat living room at the back will have to make do for our very short walk.

articles.title: How to dress a tech oligarch: The Social Reckoning’s costume designer on Zuckerberg’s style evolution
articles.summary: Susan Lyall worked with actor Jeremy Strong to research the Meta CEO’s favorite Nikes and luxury sweaters. The first Aaron Sorkin Facebook movie, 2010’s The Social Network, helped cement the early aughts image of Mark Zuckerberg rebelling against corporate norms in rumpled hoodies and T-shirts.
body: The follow-up, The Social Reckoning, is carbon-dated from 2019 to 2021. This is “post-hoodie”, as the movie’s costume designer, Susan Lyall, describes it, “post-thumbing his nose” to formality. It is also peak robot. Zuckerberg’s reserved wardrobe of suits or interchangeable long-sleeved shirts echo his chilling composure throughout, even as fury simmers under the surface.

The costume was based on deep research by Lyall and also by actor Jeremy Strong who, she says, is “very into costume”. Having worked together before, on the Sorkin movies Molly’s Game and The Trial of the Chicago 7, they would text a lot during the preparation process.

“He reaches out before I even get to reach out to him. It’s my third movie with him, so I’m pretty used to it. He’s very proactive. He’s one of my favourite actors because of that. He would know exactly where [Zuckerberg] wore what. He wanted the exact Nike shoe – the footwear was very important to him – and the exact Brunello Cucinelli T-shirt and sweater, and so on,” she says.
points: The first Aaron Sorkin Facebook movie, 2010’s The Social Network, helped cement the early aughts image of Mark Zuckerberg rebelling against corporate norms in rumpled hoodies and T-shirts.

articles.title: The last thing I did for my mother was illegal
articles.summary: An urn cost more than my rent. So I scattered my mother’s ashes at Yosemite from a Ziploc bag, without the federal permit I couldn’t afford to wait for. My mother is in a Ziploc bag on my lap, wedged between a half-eaten bag of trail mix and my purse.
body: My stomach is queasy from the switchbacks up to Yosemite, where I’ve come to spread her ashes, and I’m having an existential crisis.
I had imagined this day as a beautiful send-off that would feel profound. Instead, it was all improvisation: a plastic bag, a last-minute decision, and ginger chews to stop me from being carsick.

I thought my 20s would be about kissing the wrong people in Los Angeles bars, not reading paperbacks on a hospital cot while my mom underwent her fifth brain surgery. My friends were off at college, debating sororities and semesters abroad; I was learning an entirely different set of skills.

At 21, I learned my mom had glioblastoma, a deadly brain cancer. Soon I was in the Bakersfield law library, Googling how to become my 16-year-old brother’s legal guardian, and learning that the same charm I used to snag me a table at Nobu could also get my mom a better room at Cedars-Sinai hospital. She ended up in the room Elizabeth Taylor had died in a few weeks earlier, a detail she loved to regale her friends with.

articles.title: We’re Living in a Golden Age of Hot-Guy Politicians
articles.summary: From Zohran Mamdani and Abdul El-Sayed to Jon Ossoff and Pete Buttigieg, a new generation of politicians is going hard on policy while being easy on the eyes.
body: According to political lore, the 1960 US election was, in part, determined by hotness. That year, John F. Kennedy and Richard Nixon took part in the nation’s first televised presidential debates, giving a wide swath of the American public an alluring new metric by which to judge a could-be commander-in-chief. In one corner was the pale and clammy Nixon (who apparently refused hair and makeup on set), and in the other a freshly tanned, well-rested JFK. It’s said that those who listened on the radio assumed Nixon won, while those who caught the broadcast handily gave it to the camera-friendly Kennedy.

“Looks aren’t everything—they’re not the way we’re going to win,” says Lauren Kapp, a digital strategist who helped with Kamala Harris’s 2024 campaign. “People are focused on core issues; they’re looking for policy, and people who are talking about policy.” Still, “it’s a benefit if the person is more attractive,” she concedes. “Or if you see yourself in them.”
points: From Zohran Mamdani and Abdul El-Sayed to Jon Ossoff and Pete Buttigieg, a new generation of politicians is going hard on policy while being easy on the eyes.

articles.title: FGI’s Annual Night of Stars Gala Lit Up the Rainbow Room
articles.summary: When you bring together a group of the industry’s brightest talents in a room suspended high above New York City, you’re sure to spark greatness. On Wednesday evening, Fashion Group International (FGI) celebrated its 42nd annual Night of Stars at the Rainbow Room with a black-tie ceremony themed…
body: “Fashion Group International was founded almost 100 years ago by visionary women who understood the power of bringing creative minds together,” said Maryanne Grisz, President and CEO of Fashion Group International. “Tonight, as we celebrate extraordinary achievement, we also invest in the next generation of visionaries who will define the future of fashion, beauty, and our creative industries.”

The evening began with an elevator ascent to the 65th floor of 30 Rock, before attendees—including Vera Wang, Brandon Maxwell, and David Yurman—paraded down the red carpet and gathered for a cocktail reception set against the backdrop of panoramic views of Manhattan.

Buzzing with anticipation, the likes of Linda Fargo, Kate Barton, Fern Mallis, and designer Aiste Hong, FGI’s Rising Star of the Year recipient, caught up over Champagne to the sounds of a live string quartet. Inside the famed dining room, Vlada Roslyakova, Olympia of Greece, and Ruben Toledo took their seats at elegant round tables dressed in ivory linens and laden with fresh blooms. Once the program was underway, a dinner of rainbow chopped salad, roasted black cod, and seared beef filet awaited.

articles.title: On Location: Where was Tenzing filmed?
articles.summary: We speak with director Jennifer Peedom and actors Genden Phuntsok and Tom Hiddleston about training in the Himalayan foothills and recreating Everest on New Zealand's Mount Cook.
body: On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favorite films, television shows, and more. This time, we ask: where was Tenzing filmed?

“Some of the most impactful people live in the dip of society,” says Tibetan actor Genden Phuntsok, who plays the film's namesake, Himalayan climber Tenzing Norgay. “There aren’t many stories about what Sherpas did before the mountaineers.” In Tenzing, Peedom looks at the first ascent of Everest through the lens of Tenzing, who summited alongside New Zealand mountaineer Sir Edmund Hillary (Tom Hiddleston) after persuading Colonel John Hunt (Willem Dafoe) to give him a place on the British climbing team.

“Tenzing—as did Hillary— pushed the boundaries of what was imaginable,” says Hiddleston. “What the pair’s friendship can teach us is that there is strength in human fellowship. You begin as outsiders with different frames of reference, but we're more united by the things we share. Tenzing came from the higher Tibetan plateau, Hillary from New Zealand. They shared a love and respect for the mountains—and recognized each other.”
points: We speak with director Jennifer Peedom and actors Genden Phuntsok and Tom Hiddleston about training in the Himalayan foothills and recreating Everest on New Zealand's Mount Cook.

articles.title: The New Our Place Always Pan Is Lightweight, Nonstick, and Perfect for Weeknight Dinners
articles.summary: One of the cookware brands I come back to time and again is Our Place. I’ve been a fan of the brand’s Always Pans (both the ceramic nonstick and titanium ones) for years, as well as its air fryer-toaster oven hybrid the Wonder Oven Pro (which I seriously can’t imagine being without).
body: So when I found out that Our Place dropped a new Always Pan, I knew I needed it ASAP. And after a couple weeks of use, I can already tell it’s going to be an MVP in my kitchen.

Our Place is a relatively new brand, but in its less-than-10-year history, it’s already made a splash in the cookware scene. Its breakout product, the original Always Pan, went viral. Now the brand has multiple types of Always Pans, including the standard ceramic nonstick, enameled cast iron, and the hybrid titanium pan.

And now one of the newest additions to the collection is the Ceramic Nonstick Dual Handle Always Pan. This is different from the existing Always Pans; it looks more like a braiser with a short handle on each side, instead of a standard frying pan with a long handle. This makes it great for making one-pan dinners, browning ground beef, searing shrimp, and so much more.

Plus, the pan is 13 inches in diameter, so it’s nice and roomy, and it can be popped into an oven as hot as 450°F. The lid is also oven-safe up to 425°F. And this pan has a super-slick PFAS-free nonstick surface that works like a dream.

articles.title: Kim Kardashian Gets Hip With the LBD
articles.summary: A simple, body-conscious piece with one unusual element is straight from the Kim Kardashian playbook, and a hallmark of her recent WAG style.
body: You might think that a little black dress, one of womenswear’s greatest workhorses, can only go so far, best served as the canvas for more exciting accessories. But yesterday, Kim Kardashian made the case that the LBD can be a statement piece all by itself.

Kardashian stopped by Jimmy Kimmel Live! in Los Angeles where she wore a sculptural black maxi dress. The body-skimming scoop neck looked like something straight from Skims, save for the structural upturned peplum that jutted out from Kardashian’s hips. She kept the rest of the look sparse, only accessorizing with a pair of strappy black sandals, allowing for undivided attention to rest on her sculptural, razor thin peplum.
But in her latest look, Kardashian is going all in on her recent style codes. Even the little black dress is full of intrigue in her closet.
